explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Analysis
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. In Unit 1 you learned your first thinking skill, Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way. Well done for finishing it. Now you are ready for the second skill: Analysis.

Remember, Global Perspectives has six thinking skills. You grow them, little by little, over your years here. This unit is all about the second one:

So what is analysis? Analysis means looking closely at a topic and thinking hard about it. In research, you find things out. In analysis, you look at what you found and ask good questions about it. What do different people think? What is a fact, and what is just an opinion? Why is this happening? What pattern can I see? What would be a fair thing to do?

Why does this matter outside school? Grown-ups analyse every day. A nurse looks at what is making people ill and works out why. A shopkeeper looks at what sells and works out a pattern. A community listens to everyone before it changes a busy road. When you practise analysis now, you are learning to think clearly and be fair for the rest of your life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way. (You did this in Unit 1.)
Analysis — looking closely at what you found and asking good questions about it. (This is our unit!)
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way. This means three kinds of help all work together:

In the old way of this subject, the book kept asking learners to chat with a partner or share with the whole class. In our way, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it like a real chat. Say your ideas out loud, or type them, and let your tutor help your thinking grow.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and do the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard part, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor like a friendly study partner. It will chat about your ideas, ask you questions, and help you at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work, ask your biggest questions, and get to know the other learners.

explainers.title: Meet Karim, our analyst
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 5 learner through the whole unit. His name is Karim, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Every day at break time, the whole school comes out into one schoolyard. It gets very crowded. Some children want to play football and need lots of room to run. The younger children want a safe place to play their games. Some children just want to sit in the shade and talk. With everyone in one yard at once, footballs fly past, little children get knocked over, and arguments start.

Karim starts to wonder: why is the schoolyard so crowded at break time, and how could we make it fair and safe for everyone?

That wonder becomes Karim's project for this unit. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Karim does with it. By the end, he will have a fair plan he can share with his teacher. You will be doing the very same thing, with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: your project for the whole unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds up to one project we call your Challenge. For analysis, a good Challenge is a topic you can look at closely, where people want different things. It often happens in a shared place, or is a problem right where you live.

Here are some topics that would be great to look at closely. Any of these could be your Challenge:

Your friends care about different things. Amara, from Unit 1, still cares about clean water. Sami wishes there was more room to play football. Yasmin wants a quiet corner to read. Nadia is upset about all the litter. Any of these could grow into a Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any topic that makes you curious, or that makes you think 'that is not fair' or 'someone should fix this'. Those feelings are a great sign of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: The crowded schoolyard at break time
A busy water point where people wait in a long queue
Litter around the school or the market
A busy road that is hard to cross near school
Sharing one football pitch between many groups
Noise between neighbours in the evening
A crowded bus or a busy market on market day
Looking after the sea turtles and the fishing on the Berbera coast

explainers.title: The steps of analysis
explainers.body: Analysis comes after research. Once you have found things out, you look closely and think hard. In this unit you will learn to take these small analysis steps, one at a time:
bullets: Look at the topic from different points of view.
Sort the facts from the opinions.
Spot a pattern in your numbers.
Compare what different people think.
Find the causes and their effects.
Connect your local problem to the wider world.
Decide on a fair idea, and give a reason for it.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Look at an issue from different sides
explainers.body:
The way a person sees things is called their perspective, or point of view. Everyone sees the same thing a little differently, because of who they are and what they want. Analysis begins when you notice this.

To find the different perspectives, ask three simple questions: Who uses this place or cares about this problem? What does each person want? Why do they want it?

explainers.title: Skill 2: Tell a fact from an opinion
explainers.body:
When people talk, some of what they say is a fact, and some is an opinion. A fact is something you can check and show is true. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, and other people may disagree.

Why does this matter? To be fair, you must separate what is true from what people feel. Opinions still matter, because they tell you how people feel. But a good analyst always knows which is which. A little clue: opinions often use feeling words like best, worst, should or horrible.
bullets: Fact: Forty children come into the yard at second break. You can count them, so you can check it.
Opinion: Football is the best game in the yard. Someone else might say skipping is best.
Fact: There are two benches in the shade. You can go and look.
Opinion: Break time is horrible. That is a feeling, and not everyone feels the same.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Spot a pattern in the numbers
explainers.body:
Data means information, and it is often numbers. When you collect numbers and sort them, a pattern can appear. A pattern is something that stands out or repeats.

Karim asked his friend Nadia to help. For a few days, they counted how many children were in the yard at each break, and wrote the numbers in a table:

Now look for the pattern. The yard is much busier at second break than at the other breaks. Once Karim saw the numbers, he knew exactly when the crowding was worst. Data helped him see the pattern that his eyes alone had missed.

headers: Number of children in the yard

explainers.title: Skill 4: Compare what different people think
explainers.body:
Once you know the different points of view, it helps to line them up side by side and compare them. A simple compare grid is perfect for this. You write each group, what they want, and why.

Comparing shows you where people agree and where they disagree. Here, all three groups agree on one thing: the yard is too crowded. They only disagree about the best fix. Finding what people already agree on is a wonderful start for a fair plan.

rows: So they can play a proper game
So they do not get knocked over
So they can rest and talk

explainers.title: Skill 5: Find causes and effects
explainers.body:
Analysis asks two powerful questions: Why did this happen, and what happens because of it? The thing that makes something happen is the cause. What happens because of it is the effect.

Karim thinks carefully about the crowded yard, and finds a chain of causes and effects:

Notice the chain. One effect becomes the cause of the next thing. Finding the first cause is very powerful, because if you fix the first cause, you help all the effects that come after it.
bullets: Cause: everyone comes out at the same time. Effect: the yard is packed.
Cause: the yard is packed. Effect: children bump into each other.
Cause: children bump into each other. Effect: arguments start.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Connect your problem to the wider world
explainers.body:
Your small local problem is often part of a much bigger one in the world. Seeing this link is called making a connection. The same skill, sharing fairly, is needed everywhere, big or small.

Karim's friend Idris cares about the Berbera coast. Fishers want to catch fish there, and other people want to protect the sea turtles that lay their eggs on the same beach. Two groups, one beach, sharing fairly, just like Karim's yard.

Zara points out something even bigger. Whole towns and countries must share things too, like two towns that share one river. When you learn to share a small schoolyard fairly, you are practising something the whole world needs to get right.

That is a real connection: your crowded yard in Hargeisa is a small example of a huge idea, sharing a space fairly, that matters all over the world.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Work out a fair idea, and give a reason
explainers.body: After looking closely, you reach a conclusion: a fair idea, backed by a reason. A reason is why you think your idea is a good one. A fair idea also thinks about each group: the good parts, and the not-so-good parts. It tries to help everyone a little, even if no one gets everything they want.

explainers.title: Looking closely, and being fair
explainers.body: Analysis means seeing a topic from many sides, so being fair is part of the skill, not an extra rule. A fair analyst listens to everyone before deciding, and never leaves a group out just because they are quiet.

explainers.title: Karim's whole journey
explainers.body:
You have now met every analysis skill in this unit. Here is how Karim used them, one after another, to turn a noisy problem into a fair plan:

By looking closely and being fair, Karim turned a crowded, noisy break time into a fair plan he can share with his teacher and his school. In the Activities file, you will do the very same thing with your own Challenge, one small step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.
bullets: He looked at the crowded yard from four different points of view.
He sorted the facts from the opinions in what people said.
He counted children at each break and spotted a pattern: second break is busiest.
He made a compare grid and found what everyone agreed on.
He found the chain of causes and effects, and the first cause.
He connected his schoolyard to a bigger idea: sharing a space fairly.
He worked out a fair plan and gave a clear reason for it.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: You have now grown two big Global Perspectives skills: Research and Analysis. That is a real achievement, and you should be very proud. The next skill in the subject is Evaluation — weighing how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is. Analysis and evaluation are close partners: once you can look closely at a topic, you are ready to judge which ideas are strongest. Well done for looking closely, thinking hard, and being fair all the way through this unit.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: Research is like gathering the ingredients for a meal. Analysis is like really looking at them and working out what you can make.
In this unit we will use real topics, such as a crowded schoolyard, litter and sharing water.
But the real prize is not the topic. It is to become a clear, fair thinker who can look closely at almost anything.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to different people
lines: People live and believe in different ways, and that is a good thing to notice.

For example, the schoolyard is shared by children from many families. Some families celebrate Eid, some celebrate Christmas, and some mark other special days. A fair plan for the yard would listen to all of them, evenly.
Being fair does not mean you have no opinion. It means you listen to many people first, then work out a fair idea.

bigIdeas.title: A quick clue
lines: Opinions often use feeling words: best, worst, should, lovely, terrible, horrible.
Facts often use numbers, or things you could go and check with your own eyes.
Both matter. Opinions tell you how people feel. Facts tell you what is true. A good analyst knows which is which.

bigIdeas.title: Your three golden rules
lines: Look from more than one point of view.
Tell a fact from an opinion, and find the cause behind the problem.
Work out a fair idea, and always give a reason.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one topic you can look at closely, where people want different things. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you really care about.
By the end you will have a fair idea you can share with your teacher.

models.title: Analysis happens at home too
lines: Imagine three children in one family share a single bicycle.
You look at what each child wants: everyone wants a turn after school.
You spot the problem: only one bicycle, and everyone wants it at the same time.
You work out a fair plan: each child gets the bike on set days, with a reason everyone accepts.
That is analysis, and you already do it. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose.

models.title: Karim listens to four children about the crowded yard
lines: Sami loves football: There is never enough room to play a proper game.
Leila helps the little ones: The small children get knocked over when big kids run past.
Omar likes to rest: I just want a shady spot to sit, but every bench is full.
Nadia finds it loud: It is so noisy that I cannot hear my friends.
Four children, four perspectives. None of them is wrong. Each one has a real point of view.
A good analyst listens to all of them, not just the loudest one. The more perspectives you find, the more you understand the whole topic.

models.title: Sorting what Sami and Nadia said
lines: Sami said: Twenty of us tried to play football today. That is a fact you can count.
Sami also said: Football should get half the yard. That is an opinion.
Nadia said: I counted litter by the canteen. That is a fact.
Nadia also said: The yard is the worst place in the school. That is an opinion.

models.title: What the numbers told Karim
lines: The busiest time is second break, with 45 children.
The quietest time is first break, with 20 children.
So any fair plan should really focus on second break, because that is when the yard is most crowded.
A pattern points you straight to the real problem.

models.title: What Karim noticed from his grid
lines: Everyone agrees the yard is too crowded. That is a shared feeling he can build on.
They disagree about who needs the space most.
Because they agree on the problem, Karim is hopeful they can agree on a plan too.

models.title: Karim finds the first cause
lines: The first cause is that everyone comes out at exactly the same time.
If break times were spread out, the yard would be less packed.
Then there would be less bumping, and so fewer arguments.
Fix the first cause, and the whole chain gets better.

models.title: Karim's fair plan for the yard
lines: His idea: mark out a football corner, a quiet shade corner, and a safe area for the little ones. Let the youngest children come out one minute early.
His reason: each group gets its own space, so there is much less bumping.
Who gains: the little ones stay safe, the shade-sitters get quiet, and the footballers still get a clear area.
The not-so-good part: the football corner is a bit smaller than before. But Sami agrees it is fair, because everyone gains something.
Notice that Karim gives a reason and thinks about every group. That is what turns a quick guess into good analysis.

models.title: A model: Karim's four points of view
lines: Sami the footballer wants more room, so he can play a proper game.
Leila wants a safe corner for the little ones, so they do not get knocked over.
Omar wants a shady bench, so he can rest and talk.
Nadia wants it quieter, so she can hear her friends.

models.title: A model: Karim's chain
lines: Cause: everyone comes out at once. Effect: the yard is packed.
Cause: the yard is packed. Effect: children bump into each other.
Cause: children bump. Effect: arguments start.
The first cause is everyone coming out at once, so that is the best place to fix things.

models.title: A model: Karim's fair plan
lines: Idea: mark a football corner, a quiet shade corner, and a safe area for the little ones.
Reason: each group gets its own space, so there is much less bumping.
Who gains: the little ones are safe, the shade-sitters get quiet, and the footballers keep a clear area.
Sami is not sure at first, because his corner is smaller. Karim reminds him that everyone gains something, and that keeping the little ones safe helps the whole school.

toolkit.title: What analysis means, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Analysis means looking closely at a topic and thinking hard about it. In research, you find things out. In analysis, you look at what you found and ask good questions: What do different people think? What is a fact, and what is an opinion? Why is this happening? What pattern can I see? What would be fair?

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always look from more than one point of view, because one person only sees part of the picture. Second, always give a reason for what you think. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

Analysis and research work together. Research finds the facts and the different views; analysis looks closely at them and works out what they mean. You will use both skills side by side, all through Global Perspectives.

toolkit.title: The analysis steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your topic, good analysis follows the same simple steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel stuck.
items: Look at the topic from different points of view.
Sort the facts from the opinions.
Spot a pattern in your numbers.
Compare what different people think.
Find the causes and their effects.
Connect your local problem to the wider world.
Decide on a fair idea, and give a reason for it.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 5 Analysis goals
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out what good analysis looks like at this stage. Here are the four Analysis goals, in child-friendly words. You do not need to remember the numbers, but your teacher may talk about them, so it is helpful to know what each one means.

rows: Notice that different people see the same topic in different ways, and say what each one thinks.
Read some numbers or a chart, spot a pattern, and say what it means.
Find the causes of a problem and its effects, and link your local problem to bigger ones.
Work out a fair idea to help, and give good reasons for it.

toolkit.title: Template: Different points of view
toolkit.intro: Copy this table for your topic. For each person or group, write what they want and why. Try to fill in at least three rows.

toolkit.title: Fact or opinion check
toolkit.intro: Before you trust what someone says, ask: can I check it, or is it what they feel?

rows: Something you can check and show is true.
Forty children came into the yard.
What someone thinks or feels; others may disagree.

toolkit.title: The cause and effect arrow
toolkit.intro:
The cause is the thing that makes something happen. The effect is what happens because of it. You can join them with an arrow, like this:

Everyone comes out at once (cause) → the yard is packed (effect).

Often one effect becomes the cause of the next thing, making a chain:

Yard is packed → children bump → arguments start.

Find the first cause in the chain. If you fix the first cause, you help everything that comes after it. An effect on people is sometimes called a consequence — it is just another word for what happens because of a cause.

toolkit.title: The compare-what-people-think grid
toolkit.intro:
When two or more groups want different things, line them up side by side. Then look for what they agree on, and what they disagree about.

A shared agreement is a great place to begin a fair plan.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for analysis
toolkit.intro:
Use these to talk about points of view:

Use these to give a fair idea and a reason:
items: One person who cares about this is ...
They think ... because ...
Another person sees it differently. They think ...
These two agree that ... but they disagree about ...
After looking closely, I think we should ...
I think this because ...
This would help ... because ...
It might be hard for ..., but ...
Overall, this is fair because ...

toolkit.title: One last thing to remember
toolkit.intro: Every good thinker started exactly where you are now. You do not have to be perfect. You just have to look closely, listen to everyone, and be fair. If you get stuck, that is normal, and your AI tutor is ready to help you at any time.

checklists.title: Checklist: Is my idea fair?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, make your idea better.
items: Everyone heard — I listened to every group, even the quiet ones.
Helps each group — my idea helps every group at least a little.
Clear reason — I can say why my idea is a good one.
Thought about problems — I have thought about who might not like it.
Really possible — it is something we could actually do.

topics: Write your topic in one sentence: The topic I am looking at closely is ...

checkpoints: I was surprised to find out that ...

activities.title: Fact or opinion?
activities.label: Activity 3: Fact or opinion?
activities.intro:
A fact can be checked and shown to be true. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels. Read these six sentences. For each one, write fact or opinion. Remember the clue: opinions often use feeling words like best, worst or horrible, while facts are things you could count or check.

Then write one fact and one opinion about your own topic. Sorting facts from opinions is one of the most useful analysis skills of all, because it helps you stay fair even when people feel strongly about something.
steps: A. Forty children came into the yard at second break.
B. Football is the best game in the whole world.
C. There are two benches in the shade.
D. The canteen is the messiest place in the school.
E. Nadia counted twenty-five pieces of litter by the gate.
F. Break time is horrible.

activities.title: Spot the pattern
activities.label: Activity 4: Spot the pattern
activities.intro: Data means information, often numbers. When you sort it, a pattern can jump out at you. Here is some data: Nadia and Leila counted the litter in three places around the school one afternoon. Look at the numbers and find the pattern.
steps: Which place has the most litter? Which has the least?
Write one sentence saying what pattern you can see.
Write one idea about what might cause the litter to be worst in that place.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the pattern you found in the litter data.
Ask it whether your idea about the cause makes sense.
Then ask your tutor what numbers you could count for your own topic, to look for a pattern.

activities.title: Find the cause and the effect
activities.label: Activity 5: Find the cause and the effect
activities.intro: The cause is the thing that makes something happen. The effect is what happens because of it. Practise finding both for your own topic. Finding the very first cause is powerful, because if you fix the first cause, all the effects after it get better too.
steps: Write down one problem inside your topic.
Write the cause: why does it happen?
Write the effect: what happens because of it?
Try to make a short chain, where one effect becomes the cause of the next thing.

boxes.title: A model: Karim's chain
lines: Cause: everyone comes out at once. Effect: the yard is packed.
Cause: the yard is packed. Effect: children bump into each other.
Cause: children bump. Effect: arguments start.
The first cause is everyone coming out at once, so that is the best place to fix things.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your cause-and-effect chain to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your causes and effects are in the right order.
Then ask your tutor to help you find the very first cause in your chain.

activities.title: Compare what two groups think
activities.label: Activity 6: Compare what two groups think
activities.intro: Pick two groups who care about your topic. Make a compare grid with three columns: the group, what they want, and why. You can draw it in your notebook like this one. For example, on a busy road in Mogadishu, drivers want to travel fast and children want to cross safely. Those two groups would fill a compare grid well.
steps: Fill in what each group wants, and why.
Write one thing the two groups agree on.
Write one thing they disagree about.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your compare grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you find one more thing the two groups might agree on.
Ask your tutor why finding an agreement is a good start for a fair plan.

activities.title: Work out a fair idea, and give a reason
activities.label: Activity 7: Work out a fair idea, and give a reason
activities.intro: Now bring it all together. Work out a fair idea for your topic, give a reason, and think about each group. A fair idea tries to help everyone a little. Thinking about the good parts and the not-so-good parts for each group is what makes your idea fair, not just clever.
steps: Write your fair idea in one or two sentences.
Write your reason: why is this a good idea?
Write who gains from your idea.
Write who might not like it at first, and what you could say to them.

boxes.title: A model: Karim's fair plan
lines: Idea: mark a football corner, a quiet shade corner, and a safe area for the little ones.
Reason: each group gets its own space, so there is much less bumping.
Who gains: the little ones are safe, the shade-sitters get quiet, and the footballers keep a clear area.
Sami is not sure at first, because his corner is smaller. Karim reminds him that everyone gains something, and that keeping the little ones safe helps the whole school.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your fair idea and your reason.
Ask it whether your idea is fair to every group.
Ask your tutor to help you make your idea even fairer.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your fair idea and your reason.
Share them in your next teacher session, and ask whether your plan helps every group a little.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 12 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and use your own words.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
practice.answer: Analysis means looking closely at a topic and thinking hard about it: looking at different points of view, telling fact from opinion, spotting patterns, finding causes and effects, and working out a fair idea. (Any answer with this idea is right.)

practice.prompt: The way a person sees things, shaped by who they are and what they want, is called their ______.
practice.answer: Perspective (or point of view).

practice.prompt: Is this a fact or an opinion: 'Forty children came into the yard.'?
practice.answer: Fact (you can count the children).

practice.prompt: Is this a fact or an opinion: 'Football is the best game.'?
practice.answer: Opinion (someone else might disagree).

practice.prompt: Information, often numbers, that you collect and sort is called ______.
practice.answer: Data.

practice.prompt: Something that stands out or repeats in your data is called a ______.
practice.answer: Pattern.

practice.prompt: The thing that makes something happen is the ______. What happens because of it is the ______.
practice.answer: Cause; effect.

practice.prompt: True or false: a fair plan tries to help everyone a little, even if no one gets everything.
practice.answer: True.

practice.prompt: When you line up what different groups think, side by side, you are ______ them.
practice.answer: Comparing.

practice.prompt: Seeing how your small local problem links to a bigger one in the world is called making a ______.
practice.answer: Connection.

practice.prompt: When you give a fair idea, you should always back it up with a ______.
practice.answer: Reason.

practice.prompt: Name one word that often shows an opinion, like 'best' or 'should'.
practice.answer: Any one of: best, worst, should, terrible, horrible, lovely, better.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each analysis word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, like 1-C.
practice.prompt: Perspective
options: A. What happens because of something else.
B. The way a person sees things, shaped by who they are.
C. Something that stands out or repeats in your data.
D. Something you can check and show is true.
E. The thing that makes something happen.
F. What someone thinks or feels; others may disagree.
practice.answer: B — The way a person sees things, shaped by who they are.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Fact
practice.answer: D — Something you can check and show is true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Opinion
practice.answer: F — What someone thinks or feels; others may disagree.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Pattern
practice.answer: C — Something that stands out or repeats in your data.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Cause
practice.answer: E — The thing that makes something happen.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Effect
practice.answer: A — What happens because of something else.

practice.intro: These short stories ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Leila hears two children. One says 'Fifteen children skip rope by the wall.' The other says 'Skipping is the best game.' Which is a fact and which is an opinion? How can you tell?
practice.answer: The first is a fact, because you can count the fifteen children. The second is an opinion, because someone might not agree. The word 'best' is a clue that it is an opinion.

practice.prompt: Nadia counts the children in the yard: 20 at first break, 45 at second break, 25 at third break. What pattern can she see, and what does it tell her?
practice.answer: The pattern is that the yard is busiest at second break, with 45 children. It tells her the crowding is worst at second break, so that is where to focus a fair plan.

practice.prompt: Omar notices that everyone comes out at the same time, and then the yard is packed. Which part is the cause, and which is the effect?
practice.answer: Cause: everyone comes out at the same time. Effect: the yard is packed.

practice.prompt: Karim wants to give the little ones a safe corner, but Sami will lose a little football space. Is that fair? What could Karim say to Sami to help him accept it?
practice.answer: It can be fair, because a fair plan tries to help everyone a little. Karim could tell Sami he still keeps a marked football corner, and that keeping the little ones safe helps the whole school.

The way a person sees things, shaped by who they are and what they want.

What someone thinks or feels, which others may disagree with.
Information, often numbers, that you collect and sort.
Something that stands out or repeats in your data.
A chart where you make a mark to count each answer.
The thing that makes something happen.
What happens because of a cause.
Another word for an effect, especially on people.
To look at things side by side to see how they are alike and different.
A link between one thing and another, such as a local and a global problem.
The fair idea you reach after looking closely.
Why you think your idea is a good one.
Listening to everyone and trying to help each group a little.
A topic that people care about and may disagree on.
An idea that helps to fix a problem.

mistakes: Mixing up a fact and an opinion.
Collecting numbers but never looking for the pattern.
Saying what happened but never asking why (the cause).
Giving an idea with no reason.
Picking an idea that only helps you.
Forgetting that people can fairly disagree.
